questions.stem: A new web server image runs FTP, Telnet, and a print spooler that the web application never uses. What is the BEST hardening step?

options.rationale: Correct: fewer exposed components, fewer vulnerabilities.
Reduces exposure, but the services still run and can be reached locally.
Patching something you don't need keeps the attack surface.
Obscurity, not reduction.

questions.explanation: Reducing the surface area for attack means disabling unneeded services, ports, accounts, and software. Fewer exposed components means fewer vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: An admin must enforce a 15-minute screen lock on 3,000 Windows PCs in the domain. What BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: central enforcement across the domain.
Works, but means 3,000 separate edits.
These are domain Windows PCs.
SELinux is for Linux.

questions.explanation: Group Policy centrally manages and enforces settings on Windows computers and users.

questions.stem: A Finance PC at the HQ site receives the four conflicting settings below. Which value applies?
questions.exhibit:
Setting: Screen saver timeout
  Local policy:        30 minutes
  Site GPO (HQ):       20 minutes
  Domain GPO:          15 minutes
  OU GPO (Finance):    10 minutes

options.rationale: Correct: the OU is applied last, so it wins.
The OU GPO applies after the domain GPO.
Local applies first and is overridden.
Site comes before domain and OU.

questions.explanation: GPOs are bundles of settings linked to a site, domain, or OU. They apply in the order local, site, domain, OU, and later ones override earlier ones.
questions.discriminator_tested: Applied local, site, domain, OU; later overrides earlier.

questions.stem: What BEST describes the scope of local group policy?

options.rationale: Correct: one machine.

options.text: Settings stored on the PC itself
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't state the scope.

options.text: Settings for each PC in a domain
options.rationale: That is domain group policy.

options.text: Settings for Linux hosts via SELinux
options.rationale: Unrelated.

questions.explanation: Local group policy applies settings to a single computer; its scope is one machine.
questions.discriminator_tested: Local policy scope is one machine.

questions.stem: A PC's local policy sets a 30-minute screen lock, and a domain GPO sets 15 minutes. What BEST describes the result?

options.rationale: Correct: domain policy wins on conflict.

options.text: 30 minutes; local settings win on their own PC
options.rationale: Local applies first and is overridden.
Right result here, wrong rule: order decides, not strictness.
Conflicts are resolved by order.

questions.explanation: Domain group policy applies settings centrally to many computers and users through Active Directory. Its scope is many machines, and it overrides local settings on conflict.
questions.discriminator_tested: Domain policy overrides local on conflict.

questions.stem: A web server wrote to its uploads folder even though SELinux logged a denial for it. Given the output below, what BEST explains this?
questions.exhibit:
$ getenforce
Permissive
$ ausearch -m avc -ts recent
type=AVC msg=audit(...): avc:  denied  { write } for  pid=2211 comm="httpd" name="uploads" ...

options.text: Permissive mode logs but doesn't block
options.rationale: Correct: the denial is recorded, but the action proceeds.
True, but it doesn't say why the write succeeded.

options.text: Enforcing mode allows writes it logs
options.rationale: Enforcing mode blocks and logs.

options.text: SELinux is disabled on this server
options.rationale: Disabled wouldn't log anything; it is permissive.

questions.explanation: SELinux provides mandatory access control on Linux in three modes: enforcing, permissive, and disabled (getenforce, setenforce). Enforcing blocks and logs violations; permissive only logs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Enforcing blocks and logs; permissive only logs.

questions.stem: A Linux file server's Samba configuration is shown below. Which change BEST reduces its attack surface?
questions.exhibit:
[global]
   server min protocol = NT1
   map to guest = Bad User
[public]
   path = /srv/public
   guest ok = yes
   writable = yes

options.text: Require SMB2+ and remove guest write access
options.rationale: Correct: drops SMBv1 and anonymous writing.

options.text: Keep Samba patched to the latest release
options.rationale: Good practice, but it leaves SMBv1 and guest write enabled.
A new name doesn't change access.

options.text: Open TCP 445 to the internet for testing
options.rationale: That increases exposure.

questions.explanation: Samba is the Linux/Unix implementation of SMB file and print sharing. Exposed SMB is attack surface: disable it if unused, restrict shares, require authentication, disable SMBv1, and keep it patched.
questions.discriminator_tested: Restrict shares, require authentication, disable SMBv1.

questions.stem: Assessment results must be presented to both the board and the engineering team. What is the BEST approach to the report?

options.rationale: Correct: tailored to each audience.

options.text: One detailed technical report for both
options.rationale: Serves engineers, but loses the board.

options.text: Raw scanner output for both groups
options.rationale: Useful to no one without analysis.

options.text: A verbal briefing with nothing written
options.rationale: Leaves no record.

questions.explanation: Security reports summarize assessment findings, vulnerabilities, and recommendations. Tailor them to the audience: technical detail versus an executive summary.

questions.stem: A blog post claims a new attack affects every router in the world. What should the security team do FIRST?

options.rationale: Correct: verify credibility before acting.

options.text: Check their router models against it
options.rationale: A sensible next step once the claim is confirmed.
Drastic, on an unverified claim.

options.text: Ignore it, since blogs are unreliable
options.rationale: Some are credible; verify instead.

questions.explanation: Cybersecurity news sources report emerging threats and vulnerabilities. They build awareness, but their credibility must be verified.

questions.stem: What BEST describes what a paid threat-intelligence subscription typically offers over free news sources?

options.rationale: Correct, at a cost.
Free sources offer that too.
Intelligence informs; it doesn't patch.
Information can't prevent breaches by itself.

questions.explanation: Subscription-based sources are paid or subscribed threat-intelligence feeds and advisories. They are curated, timely, and often deeper than free sources, but they cost money.

questions.stem: An analyst wants new advisories from ten vendor websites delivered automatically, without visiting each site. What BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: pulls new items automatically.
Scans hosts, not websites' news.
Still visiting each site.
Correlates logs, not web content.

questions.explanation: An RSS feed delivers new items from chosen sites automatically. It pulls updates to you without visiting each site.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why documenting processes matters for security work?

options.rationale: Correct.
A side benefit, not the core reason.

options.text: It replaces the need for training
options.rationale: Documents support training; they don't replace it.
Documentation doesn't encrypt.

questions.explanation: Documentation is a written record of processes, changes, and events. It makes actions repeatable and auditable.

questions.stem: During an outage, responders followed the network diagram, which still showed a firewall replaced a year ago. The fix was delayed by hours. What BEST describes the root cause?

options.rationale: Correct: the diagram wasn't kept current.
They did what the documents said.

options.text: The diagram was hard to read
options.rationale: Readable but wrong is still wrong.
Nothing suggests that.

questions.explanation: Updating documentation means keeping documents current as systems, processes, and lessons change. Outdated documentation misleads responders.

questions.stem: An incident record reads as shown below. What BEST describes the problem with it?
questions.exhibit:
Incident IR-0912 log
- Someone noticed odd traffic.
- The server was unplugged at some point.
- Malware was removed.

options.text: It lacks times, systems, and names
options.rationale: Correct: it isn't a factual, time-stamped account.
Length isn't the issue; missing facts are.

options.text: It should be kept by the vendor
options.rationale: The organization keeps its own records.
It includes far too little.

questions.explanation: Security incident documentation records the timeline, affected systems, actions taken, and who did what. It is a factual, time-stamped account.

questions.stem: A forensic case has the custody log below. What is the MOST serious problem?
questions.exhibit:
Item: laptop LT-0457    Case IR-0912
10/03 09:14   collected by J. Ortiz       sealed bag #5521
10/03 11:40   received by evidence room   bag #5521
10/05 15:20   received by forensic lab    bag #5873

options.text: No entry shows who moved it, and the bag changed
options.rationale: Correct: a gap in the trail undermines the evidence.

options.text: The lab received it two days later
options.rationale: The delay matters less than the undocumented handling.

options.text: The laptop wasn't imaged at collection
options.rationale: Not shown, and not the custody issue.

options.text: The evidence room should sign twice
options.rationale: There's no such rule.

questions.explanation: Chain of custody is the documented trail of who handled evidence, when, and how. A gap undermines the integrity and admissibility of the evidence.
questions.discriminator_tested: A gap undermines integrity and admissibility.

questions.stem: A breach exposes customer data in a region whose regulation requires notification within 72 hours. What is the BEST action for the incident lead?

options.rationale: Correct: the defined path, and the legal deadline.
Necessary, but not the whole reporting obligation.

options.text: Wait until the investigation is complete
options.rationale: That could miss the mandated deadline.

options.text: Post the details on social media first
options.rationale: Not a defined reporting path.

questions.explanation: Reporting incidents means notifying the right parties (management, security, legal, regulators, customers) per policy. Follow the defined reporting path; some timing is mandated by regulation.
questions.discriminator_tested: Follow the reporting path; some timing is mandated.

questions.stem: A ransomware infection has been contained. Which order of recovery steps is correct?

options.text: Restore from clean backups, validate, return to service
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Return to service, then restore, then validate
options.rationale: Systems go live before they are restored.

options.text: Validate, return to service, then restore
options.rationale: Nothing to validate before restoring.

options.text: Restore from the newest backup, even if infected
options.rationale: An infected backup reinfects.

questions.explanation: Incident recovery restores affected systems to normal operation: clean backups, rebuild, validate. It returns systems to service after containment.
questions.discriminator_tested: Return to service after containment, from clean sources.

questions.stem: What BEST describes the purpose of a post-incident review?

options.rationale: Correct: improvement, not blame.
True, but it misses the aim.
That is recovery.
Reviews aim at improvement, not blame.

questions.explanation: Reviewing the incident is a post-incident review to find the root cause and improve controls. It happens after recovery and aims at improvement, not blame.

questions.stem: Which two are documentation best practices during an incident? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct: document as you go.

options.text: Storing records securely, with access control
options.rationale: Correct: records can contain sensitive details.

options.text: Rewriting the log at the end for clarity
options.rationale: Loses accuracy and timeliness.

options.text: Keeping notes in a personal email account
options.rationale: Not secure or controlled.

options.text: Leaving out times to save effort
options.rationale: Timestamps are essential.

questions.explanation: Documentation best practices: clear, accurate, timely, consistent, version-controlled, and securely stored. Document as you go, and protect the documents because they can contain sensitive details.
questions.discriminator_tested: Document as you go; protect the documents.
